name: Command
intent: Turn a request into an object, so it can be queued, logged, and undone.
scenario: A text editor has Insert and Uppercase actions. Users expect Undo and Redo for both.
problem: When buttons call document methods directly, nothing remembers what was done. Undo would need every action to know how to reverse itself in some ad-hoc way, and the UI would need to know about each action.
solution: Wrap each action in a Command object with execute() and undo(). A History (the invoker) runs commands and keeps them on two stacks. Undo pops the last command and calls its undo(); redo reruns it. The History never needs to know what any command does.
pain: The UI calls document methods directly
No record of what happened, so no undo
Each new action needs custom undo logic scattered in the UI
Actions cannot be queued, replayed or logged
benefits: Every action is an object with execute() and undo()
Undo and redo work for every command with one History class
Commands can be queued, logged, replayed or batched
A new action is a new command, with no changes to History
whenToUse: You need undo/redo, history, or macros
You want to queue, schedule or log operations
You want to decouple whoever triggers an action from whoever performs it
whenNotToUse: Actions are trivial and never need undoing or recording
Undo is impossible for the operation (sending an email)
pitfalls: Many tiny classes: one per action
Commands must capture enough state to undo, which can be large
Undo logic is easy to get subtly wrong
Redo history must be cleared when a new command runs after undo

roles.label: Invoker
roles.description: Runs commands and keeps the history (here: History).

roles.label: Concrete Command
roles.description: One specific action plus what it needs to reverse itself.

roles.label: Receiver
roles.description: The object the commands act on (here: Document).

quiz.question: An editor's Uppercase action turns 'Hello World' into 'HELLO WORLD'. The team writes its undo as 'convert the text to lowercase'. What goes wrong, and what is the fix?
options: Nothing goes wrong, since lowercase is the exact inverse of uppercase for any text
Case information is lost, so execute() should save the original text and undo() restore it
The undo should run only on short texts, to avoid keeping large copies in the history
The undo should be removed, because commands that change case cannot be undone
quiz.explanation: Uppercase loses information, so the original casing cannot be derived from the result. A command must capture the state it needs at execute time and restore it on undo. Lowercase is not an inverse, and the action can be undone with saved state.

quiz.question: A History keeps an undo stack and a redo stack. The user inserts A, inserts B, presses Undo (B is undone), then inserts C. They press Redo. What should happen?
options: Both B and C are applied again, in the order they were created
B is re-applied after C, since it was the last command that was undone
C is removed and B is re-applied, as redo always follows the latest undo
Nothing, since running the new command C should have cleared the redo stack
quiz.explanation: After a new command, the old future no longer matches the document, so redo history must be cleared. Re-applying B would run it against a state it was never designed for and could corrupt the text.

quiz.question: A macro command runs three commands in order: A, B, C. C throws an error after A and B have already run. The editor wants the document back to its starting state. What should the macro do?
options: Call undo on A, then on B, in the same order in which they ran
Leave A and B applied and record the macro as done, since two of its three steps worked
Retry C until it succeeds, so that the macro finishes the way it was planned
Undo B then A, in reverse order, and do not record the macro in the history
quiz.explanation: Undo must run in reverse order, because B may depend on A's result. Undoing in forward order can restore the wrong state. Keeping partial work leaves the document half changed, and endless retries may never succeed.
